llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: This paper introduces Any-Precision LLM for low-cost deployment of multiple, different-sized Large Language Models (LLMs) by extending the concept of any-precision Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to LLMs. It addresses the challenges of memory overhead and high training costs associated with deploying multiple LLMs of varying sizes. The key contributions include a lightweight post-training quantization (PTQ) method for any-precision LLM, utilizing incremental upscaling based on non-uniform quantization (SqueezeLLM), and a specialized software engine. This solution significantly reduces deployment costs by packing LLMs quantized to various bit-widths (e.g., 3 to n bits) into a memory footprint comparable to a single n-bit LLM (up to 3.56x memory savings for Llama-2-7B). The approach maintains state-of-the-art model quality across different bit-widths and achieves high inference throughput, matching or outperforming existing quantized matrix-vector multiplication engines that lack any-precision support, by leveraging a bitplane-based memory layout and GPU kernel optimizations.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology involves a two-stage any-precision quantization scheme called incremental upscaling and a specialized software engine. The quantization process starts with a 'seed model generation' where the LLM is quantized to the minimum supported bit-width (n1) using a post-training quantization (PTQ) framework. Subsequently, 'incremental upscaling' is performed, where the model is progressively upscaled one bit at a time to higher bit-widths (up to nK), by inheriting parameters and appending an additional bit to each. This process leverages SqueezeLLM, a clustering-based non-uniform quantization method, which is compatible with incremental upscaling by dividing existing clusters into two sub-clusters using weighted K-means and a sensitivity metric. The specialized software engine adopts a bitplane-based representation for quantized weights, which allows loading only the necessary bits for a given precision, enabling proportional speedups. It includes three GPU kernel optimization techniques: Weight Bitplane Layout Optimization (WLO) for coalesced memory access, an Efficient Bit-transpose (IBT) algorithm for reducing bitwise operations, and Merging Table Lookups (TLM) for calculating centroid indices more efficiently, especially at lower bit-widths. For large batch sizes (e.g., prefill phase), the engine dequantizes weights with a separate kernel and then uses the cuBLAS FP16 kernel.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The research evaluated LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B, and three OPT models (6.7B, 2.7B, 1.3B). Any-precision models from 4 to 8 bits were generated via incremental upscaling from a 3-bit SqueezeLLM seed model and compared against independently quantized SqueezeLLM models. Perplexity was measured on WikiText2, C4, and Penn Treebank (PTB) datasets. Zero-shot accuracy was evaluated on five tasks: ARC-easy/challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande, using the Language Model Evaluation Harness framework. Kernel microbenchmarks for matrix-vector multiplication latency were conducted on RTX 4090 (desktop), RTX 4070 Laptop (laptop), and Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB (mobile) GPUs, comparing against the SqueezeLLM kernel and cuBLAS FP16 baseline using NVIDIA Nsight Compute. An ablation study assessed the impact of WLO, IBT, and TLM. Matrix-matrix multiplication performance with small batch sizes (2, 4, 8) and large M values was also evaluated. End-to-end inference throughput was measured by integrating the engine with TensorRT-LLM, generating 128 and 1024 tokens on RTX 4090 and RTX 4070 Laptop.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Direct application of existing any-precision DNN methods (Yu et al., 2021) to LLMs is problematic because they are quantization-aware training (QAT) schemes, requiring costly training from scratch for LLMs. Furthermore, these methods do not inherently provide memory bandwidth savings for lower bit-widths, limiting actual inference speedups for memory-bound LLMs. The study also found that state-of-the-art uniform quantization methods like GPTQ and AWQ are not suitable for incremental upscaling due to significant quality degradation and incompatibility with the incremental upscaling process, making them unfavorable for any-precision support. Lastly, for very large batch sizes or sequence lengths (e.g., during the prefill phase with large M), the specialized kernel may be slower than the cuBLAS FP16 baseline due to its lack of tensor core utilization, necessitating a switch to cuBLAS to mitigate performance slowdowns.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Token-level dynamic quantization has shown promise for saving memory/latency, yet two road-blocks remain: (1) on today’s GPUs only one fixed weight precision can be used per matrix multiply, so existing methods vary the *activation* precision only, leaving most of the potential untapped; (2) deciding per-token precision with minimal overhead is hard – current heuristics (norm, entropy, gradient proxy) either add latency or miss hard-to-quantise tokens, degrading reasoning accuracy (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K). A solution that can  • load exactly the required weight bit-planes at run-time (any-precision execution)  • while predicting token importance fast enough to hide its cost could unlock truly context-adaptive LLMs with sub-4-bit average precision – something no prior work has demonstrated on end-to-end LLM inference.
Methods: We propose HATQ (Hardware-Aware Token-adaptive Quantization):
1. Bit-Plane Ready Weights – starting from a 3-bit SqueezeLLM seed, apply incremental upscaling to 8-bit, storing weights as separate bit-planes (Any-Precision LLM).  All bit-planes are kept on GPU but can be loaded selectively.
2. Hierarchical Precision Controller – a two-stage lightweight network that predicts, for every new token, (a) a *layer-global budget* in bits/timestep using an RNN over recent KV activations (~0.1 ms), and (b) a *per-token mask* within that budget via a single transformer block that re-uses the model’s last-layer hidden states (no extra KV-cache).
3. Budgeted Bit-Plane Fetch – extend the Any-Precision GPU kernels with:  • masked bit-plane loading (load most-significant 2–3 bit-planes for all tokens; fetch additional planes only for tokens flagged by the controller);  • micro-batch splitting so that different tokens in the same batch may call the kernel with different effective precisions without serialisation.
4. Joint Fine-Tuning – freeze original weights, train only centroids (like QuIP re-ordering) and the precision controller on 2 k mixed-domain sequences with a loss = λ· ppl + (1–λ)· latency proxy (differentiable through a straight-through estimator over bit counts).
5. Drop-in BitsAndBytes interface – implement as nn.Linear subclass that chooses at forward() time which planes to read, maintaining compatibility with HF pipelines.
Experimental Setup: Models: Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B (CUDA 11.8, A100-80G)
Datasets / Tasks:
• Perplexity – WikiText-2, C4  • Reasoning – MMLU 57-subjects, GSM8K few-shot  • Commonsense – HellaSwag
Baselines: FP16, static 4-bit RTN, AWQ (4-bit), SqueezeLLM-3/4-bit, Any-Precision 4-bit (no dynamics), CherryQ-3-bit.
Metrics:
• Accuracy/F1 on downstream tasks  • Perplexity  • tokens/sec generation for 16, 128, 512 prompt+generation lengths  • GPU peak memory  • Effective average weight bits (computed from bit-plane counts).
Ablations: (i) controller off (falls back to 4-bit) (ii) only global budget, no token mask (iii) fetch cost without kernel optimisations.
Robustness: evaluate on adversarially perturbed prompts (AdvBench) and long-context (32k) synthetic copying task.
Result: Expected:  • Same MMLU accuracy as static 4-bit (−0.1 pt) while reducing effective precision to 2.8–3.2 bits.  • 18-25 % higher tokens/sec and 12-15 % lower peak memory v.s. static 4-bit; 45-50 % faster than FP16.  • Controller overhead <2 % of total latency.  • On adversarial / long-context tests accuracy drops <1 %, showing stability.
Ablation (i) reverts speed to static; (ii) yields only half the gain, showing need for token mask; (iii) proves new kernels save ~10 %.
Conclusion: HATQ bridges the algorithm–hardware gap for context-adaptive precision: by pairing a learned hierarchical controller with bit-plane kernels it is the first to vary *weight* precision per token at run-time on commodity GPUs. The result is a Pareto improvement in memory, speed and accuracy, enabling cheaper deployment of reasoning-heavy LLM services and opening the door to further research on learned precision schedules, cross-model transfer of controllers, and integration with speculative decoding or on-device mobile GPUs. Future work can explore extending HATQ to training-time cyclic precision and to 2-bit base models using COLLEGE-style MCF error compensation.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Below are three complementary, implementable experimental plans to validate HATQ from algorithmic, systems, and end-to-end perspectives. Each plan includes model/dataset setup, procedures, metrics, ablations, and minimal Python scaffolding.

Experiment 1 — End-to-end effectiveness on accuracy, speed, memory, and average bits
Goal
- Demonstrate HATQ’s Pareto improvement: static-4b accuracy with lower effective weight bits, higher tokens/sec, and lower peak memory across diverse tasks and sequence lengths.

Setup
- Hardware: 1× A100-80GB (CUDA 11.8), PyTorch 2.1+, Triton 2.1+ (optional for kernels), HF Transformers 4.41+.
- Models: Llama-2-7B-hf and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2.
- Quantized weight seed: SqueezeLLM 3-bit checkpoints or reproduce 3-bit with SqueezeLLM tool; run incremental upscaling to 8-bit and pack as per-bit planes.
- Datasets/Tasks:
  - Perplexity: WikiText-2, C4 (validation splits).
  - Reasoning: MMLU (57 subjects), GSM8K few-shot (8-shot standard prompts).
  - Commonsense: HellaSwag (10-shot).
  - Robustness: AdvBench prompts (subset) and 32k synthetic copy task.
- Baselines: FP16; static 4-bit RTN; AWQ 4-bit; SqueezeLLM 3/4-bit; Any-Precision 4-bit (no dynamics); CherryQ 3-bit.

Key HATQ components
- Bit-plane weights: W = sum_{b=0..7} 2^b · B_b, B_b in {−1, +1} (or packed int1/int2 slices), with 3 MSBs guaranteed from SqueezeLLM and extra planes learned/packed.
- Hierarchical precision controller:
  - Stage A (global): small GRU/LSTM over recent layer-wise KV statistics emits layer-global bit budget per step (in bits per token).
  - Stage B (per-token): 1 transformer block reading last-layer hidden states produces token-level masks within the budget.
- Budgeted bit-plane fetch: kernel chooses MSB planes for all tokens and conditionally fetches more planes for flagged tokens; micro-batch split groups tokens by bit-count.

Procedure
1) Prepare bit-plane weights (preprocessing):
   - Load SqueezeLLM-3b weights; compute centroids and pack MSBs.
   - Learn/pack additional planes up to 8-bit using incremental upscaling with centroid re-ordering (freeze original weights; train only centroids as in QuIP-style reordering) on a 2k mixed-domain set.
2) Plug-in HATQLinear (nn.Linear subclass) via monkey-patching or model surgery so HF pipelines remain unchanged.
3) Train the controller jointly with centroid re-ordering on 2k sequences (length 2k), objective: L = λ·NLL + (1−λ)·LatencyProxy, with straight-through on bit counts.
   - λ ≈ 0.8; optimizer AdamW lr=2e-4, 10k steps, cosine decay, batch=8 sequences.
4) Inference loops:
   - Measure tasks at prompt+gen lengths: {16, 128, 512} total tokens.
   - For each task:
     - Warm-up 50 steps to stabilize clocks; then time end-to-end generation/evaluation.
     - Log tokens/sec, peak memory, effective average weight bits, accuracy/F1/perplexity.
     - Record controller latency contribution per step.
5) Robustness:
   - AdvBench: evaluate subset (e.g., 200 prompts), compare accuracy/behavior under precision schedules.
   - Long-context: run synthetic 32k repeat-and-recall task; measure accuracy vs position.

Metrics
- Accuracy/F1: MMLU macro-avg, GSM8K exact-match, HellaSwag acc.
- Perplexity: WT2, C4.
- Throughput: tokens/sec (decode-only), for lengths {16, 128, 512}.
- GPU peak memory: torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().
- Effective average weight bits: avg over steps,layers,tokens of bit-planes fetched.
- Controller overhead: ratio of controller time to total step time.

Ablations
- (i) Controller off ⇒ fixed 4-bit (same bit-plane packing, no dynamics).
- (ii) Only global budget, no token mask.
- (iii) Disable kernel optimizations: force loading all planes then mask in compute (measures fetch inefficiency).

Expected outcomes
- Accuracy within −0.1 pt of static 4b on MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag.
- Effective bits 2.8–3.2 on average with 18–25% tokens/sec gain vs static 4b; 12–15% lower peak memory.
- Controller overhead <2%.
- Ablations show (ii) recovers about half speedup; (iii) loses ~10% tokens/sec.

Minimal Python scaffolding (illustrative)
- HATQLinear forward (bit-plane selection, grouping, counters):

  class HATQLinear(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, in_f, out_f, planes=8, packer=None):
          super().__init__()
          self.in_f, self.out_f = in_f, out_f
          self.planes = planes
          # Packed bit-planes: list of [out_f, in_f] int8 tensors with values in {−1, +1}
          self.B = nn.ParameterList([nn.Parameter(torch.empty(out_f, in_f, dtype=torch.int8), requires_grad=False) for _ in range(planes)])
          self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(out_f), requires_grad=False)
          self.register_buffer("bit_counters", torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.long), persistent=False)

      def forward(self, x, token_bits_per_layer):
          # x: [T, B, in_f]; token_bits_per_layer: [T, B] ints in [2..8]
          # Group tokens by bit-count for micro-batch split
          T, B, D = x.shape
          x2 = x.view(T*B, D)
          bits = token_bits_per_layer.view(-1)
          unique_bits = torch.unique(bits)
          out = torch.empty(T*B, self.out_f, device=x.device, dtype=torch.float16)
          for k in unique_bits.tolist():
              idx = (bits == k).nonzero(as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
              xk = x2.index_select(0, idx)
              # Matmul with MSBs and optional extra planes
              # Base: use planes p in [planes-k, planes)
              base = None
              for p in range(self.planes - k, self.planes):
                  wk = self.B[p].to(torch.float16)
                  contrib = xk @ wk.t()
                  base = contrib if base is None else base + (2**p) * contrib
              out.index_copy_(0, idx, base)
          self.bit_counters += bits.sum().cpu()
          return (out * self.scale)

- Controller call and bit logging:

  def step_controller(layer_stats, last_hidden):
      # returns per-layer budget and per-token masks
      # dummy placeholder; replace with trained modules
      global_bits = torch.clamp((layer_stats.mean(-1) * 4 + 3).round(), 2, 8).int()
      token_mask = (last_hidden.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=False) > 3.0)  # boolean [T,B]
      return global_bits, token_mask

  def effective_bits(global_bits, token_mask, min_msb=3):
      # ensure MSB floor and allocate extra for masked tokens
      gb = torch.clamp(global_bits, min=min_msb)
      extra = (token_mask.int())
      return torch.clamp(gb + extra, max=8)

- Throughput/memory harness:

  def bench(run_fn, warmup=50, steps=200):
      start, end = [torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for _ in range(2)]
      for _ in range(warmup): run_fn()
      torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
      start.record()
      for _ in range(steps): run_fn()
      end.record(); end.synchronize()
      ms = start.elapsed_time(end)
      mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()
      return ms/steps, mem


Experiment 2 — Systems micro-benchmarks of masked bit-plane fetch and micro-batch splitting
Goal
- Isolate and quantify the kernel-level benefits: selective bit-plane loading and token grouping vs static kernels and naïve dynamic execution.

Setup
- Synthetic GEMM shapes mirroring LLM layers: e.g., (M, K, N) = (32–1024 tokens, 4096, 4096) and feed-forward shapes (K=11008, N=4096), int8-packed bit-planes.
- Implement two execution modes:
  1) Static 4-bit GEMM (baseline): read fixed MSB planes for all tokens.
  2) HATQ masked fetch: read MSB planes for all tokens; conditionally read extra planes only for selected tokens per step, using micro-batch splitting (group tokens by bit budget) and/or a Triton kernel that supports per-row plane masks.
  3) Naïve dynamic: per-precision serial kernel calls without grouping (upper bound on overhead).
  4) Fetch-without-optimizations: load all planes then mask in compute (ablation iii).

Procedure
- Generate budget distributions to emulate realistic workloads, e.g.:
  - Mix A: 70% 3-bit, 25% 4-bit, 5% 6-bit tokens.
  - Mix B: 85% 3-bit, 10% 4-bit, 5% 7-bit tokens.
  - Mix C (adversarial): 10% 3-bit, 60% 4-bit, 30% 6-bit tokens.
- For each mix, run M in {32, 128, 512} tokens, average over 100 runs.
- Metrics: kernel time, achieved FLOPs, DRAM GB/s, bytes loaded per matmul (analytical and measured), tokens/sec equivalent.
- Optional: profile with Nsight Systems/Compute for occupancy and memory transactions.

Minimal Python/Triton scaffold (illustrative signatures)

  # Triton kernel signature (pseudo):
  @triton.jit
  def hatq_gemm_bitplanes(A_ptr, B_planes_ptr, C_ptr, M, N, K, plane_mask_ptr, stride params ...):
      # plane_mask_ptr: [M] bitmask per row; load planes conditionally
      # ... implement tile loops; for each plane p: if mask bit set or p in MSB set then load
      pass

  # Python driver for grouping and dispatch:
  def run_grouped(A, B_planes, bit_counts):
      # A: [M,K], B_planes: list of [N,K] per plane, bit_counts: [M]
      outs = torch.empty(A.size(0), B_planes[0].size(0), device=A.device, dtype=torch.float16)
      for k in torch.unique(bit_counts):
          idx = (bit_counts == k).nonzero().squeeze(-1)
          Ak = A.index_select(0, idx).contiguous()
          mask = torch.zeros(Ak.size(0), dtype=torch.int32, device=A.device)  # encode extra planes
          # call Triton kernel with per-row mask derived from k
          hatq_gemm_bitplanes[grid](Ak, B_planes, outs.index_select(0, idx), ...)
      return outs

- Measurement helper:

  def time_kernel(fn, iters=200):
      s = torch.cuda.Event(True); e = torch.cuda.Event(True)
      for _ in range(20): fn()
      s.record();
      for _ in range(iters): fn()
      e.record(); e.synchronize();
      return s.elapsed_time(e)/iters

Comparisons
- Static 4-bit vs HATQ masked vs Naïve dynamic vs Fetch-without-opt.
- Report speedup vs static 4-bit and bytes saved.

Expected outcomes
- Masked fetch + grouping reduces bytes read by 25–40% under Mix A/B, yielding ~10–20% kernel-time speedup; naïve dynamic performs much worse due to serialization; ablation (fetch-without-opt) confirms ~10% penalty, isolating benefit of selective loading.


Experiment 3 — Controller quality, overhead, and ablations vs heuristics
Goal
- Show the hierarchical controller predicts precision needs accurately, generalizes across domains, and adds negligible overhead, outperforming heuristics.

Setup
- Data for training: 2k mixed-domain sequences (C4, Wikipedia, Code, QA), length 2k.
- Labels for diagnostics: offline compute a per-token difficulty proxy by measuring delta in NLL/logit error when adding 2 extra bit-planes to a 3-bit base on a held-out set.
- Models: Same as Experiment 1; freeze model weights and train centroids + controller.

Training objective
- Joint: L = λ·NLL + (1−λ)·LatencyProxy.
- LatencyProxy: proportional to expected bit-plane bytes per step, e.g., sum_t,l E[b_{t,l}] / budget_norm.
- Straight-through estimator: discretize bit counts during forward; backprop through a sigmoid-softplus relaxation during backward.

Baselines for decision policy
- Heuristics: token norm, entropy of logits, gradient proxy (per-token loss increment), random.
- Reduced HATQ: (i) controller off, (ii) only global budget.

Procedure
1) Offline label creation:
   - For a held-out 200-sequence set, for each token, compute NLL at 3b and 3b+Δ (e.g., +2 bits). Define y=1 if ΔNLL < −τ (token benefits from more bits) with τ chosen to select ~10–20% of tokens.
2) Train controller:
   - Stage A: small GRU (64–128 hidden) over per-layer KV stats from last 16 steps; output per-layer budgets in [2..8].
   - Stage B: 1 transformer block (hidden 256, 2 heads) over last-layer hidden states; output token mask logit per step; project to extra bits under global budget via knapsack-like differentiable selection.
   - Hyperparams: AdamW lr=2e-4, wd=0.01, 10k steps, batch=8, grad-clip 1.0.
3) Diagnostics on a 500-sequence dev set:
   - ROC-AUC/F1 of token-mask vs offline labels.
   - Correlation between predicted budgets and measured quantization error.
   - Overhead: time forward pass of controller (CUDA graph capture to reduce latency), target <0.1 ms for Stage A and <0.8 ms for Stage B at 7B scale.
4) Policy-to-metric impact:
   - Plug each policy into HATQLinear and measure tokens/sec vs accuracy trade-off on WT2, MMLU-5-subset, GSM8K-500.
   - Plot accuracy vs effective bits; compare areas under curve.
5) Generalization and transfer:
   - Train controller on Llama-2-7B, evaluate zero-shot on Mistral-7B without re-tuning; report deltas.

Metrics
- Token-level: ROC-AUC, Precision/Recall@k for “hard” tokens.
- End-to-end: accuracy deltas at matched effective bits, tokens/sec at matched accuracy.
- Overhead: controller wall-clock per step and % of step time.

Minimal Python scaffold for STE bit budgeting

  class BudgetHead(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, min_bits=3, max_bits=8):
          super().__init__(); self.min_bits=min_bits; self.max_bits=max_bits
      def forward(self, logits):
          # logits: [T,B] unconstrained; use relaxed rounding
          probs = torch.sigmoid(logits)
          cont = self.min_bits + (self.max_bits-self.min_bits)*probs  # [T,B]
          if self.training:
              noise = torch.empty_like(cont).uniform_(-0.5, 0.5)
              hard = torch.clamp((cont + noise).round(), self.min_bits, self.max_bits)
          else:
              hard = torch.clamp(cont.round(), self.min_bits, self.max_bits)
          # STE: forward uses hard; backward uses cont
          return hard.detach() + (cont - cont.detach())

  def latency_proxy(bits):
      # bits: [T,B,L] predicted per-layer bits; approximate bytes ~ sum(bits)
      return bits.float().mean()

Expected outcomes
- Controller achieves ROC-AUC > 0.8 vs offline labels; improves accuracy-at-fixed-bits vs heuristics; overhead <2% of step time.
- Ablations confirm both global budget and token mask are necessary; heuristics either miss hard tokens or over-allocate bits.


Notes and implementation tips
- Bit-plane packing: for prototyping, store planes as int8 tensors with values ±1 and multiply by 2^p scales; later replace with actual packed bit tensors and Triton kernels.
- CUDA Graphs: capture decode loop after a few warmup steps to reduce launch overhead, ensuring controller ops are graph-compatible or executed in a side stream.
- Effective bits accounting: maintain per-layer counters of fetched planes; compute avg_bits = total_fetched_planes / (num_tokens * num_layers).
- Sequence-length sensitivity: ensure KV-cache bandwidth is not the bottleneck when interpreting tokens/sec; report both compute-only kernel time and end-to-end time.
- Reproducibility: fix seeds, enable deterministic algorithms where possible, and report driver/library versions.

Together, these three experiments validate HATQ’s algorithm–hardware contributions: (1) end-to-end Pareto gains; (2) kernel-level efficiency from masked bit-plane fetch and micro-batch splitting; (3) a fast, accurate hierarchical controller that outperforms heuristics with negligible overhead.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below I expand each experiment in the Experiment Strategy, adding concrete implementation details, reliability practices, and minimal PyTorch/Triton scaffolding. I integrate overlapping verification items where possible (e.g., end-to-end KPIs and robustness in Experiment 1; kernel contributions in Experiment 2; decision policy quality and overhead in Experiment 3). All code examples assume PyTorch, Hugging Face, and Triton; I favor existing libraries over from-scratch implementations.

Global prerequisites
- Hardware/Software
  - 1× A100-80GB (PCIe or SXM), CUDA 11.8, cuDNN 8.9+, driver 535+.
  - PyTorch 2.1+, Triton 2.1+, Transformers 4.41+, Accelerate 0.33+, BitsAndBytes 0.43+, datasets 2.20+, evaluate 0.4+, lm-eval 0.4.2+, flash-attn 2.5+ (optional but recommended for attention kernels in end-to-end evals).
  - Optional: Nsight Systems/Compute for profiling; wandb or tensorboard for logging.
- Reproducibility
  - Fix random seeds across torch, numpy, random; set deterministic algorithms where feasible (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)) for evaluation-only runs.
  - Log exact package versions and GPU clocks. Warm-up kernels before timing; disable boost clocks or pin clocks for stable measurements if possible.
- Datasets (HF datasets)
  - wikitext-2-raw-v1 for perplexity; c4 (validation subset); hellaswag; gsm8k; mmlu (via lm-eval or hf mirror); AdvBench subset; synthetic long-context generation you create on-the-fly.
- Baseline models
  - Llama-2-7B-hf and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (or Mistral-7B-v0.1 for non-instruct). Use identical tokenizers across variants.

Bit-plane weights preparation (shared for all experiments)
- Start from a SqueezeLLM 3-bit model (seed). If not available, run SqueezeLLM quantization to 3-bit per-channel/per-group weights on the FP16 model. Store centroids and assignment codes.
- Incremental upscaling to 8-bit bit-planes
  - Concept: represent weight W as sum over planes: W ≈ sum_{p=0..7} s_p · B_p, with B_p ∈ {−1,+1} at plane p; s_p are global or per-row scales consolidating centroid re-ordering (QuIP style) for MSB correctness. We guarantee top 3 planes match the 3-bit SqueezeLLM seed; the remaining planes add fine detail.
  - Freeze the original model’s FP weights; train only plane scales/centroids/reordering (very small parameter set) on a mixed-domain 2k-sequence corpus. This keeps memory low and avoids catastrophic drift.
- Storage format for prototyping
  - Use 8 tensors [out_features, in_features] dtype=int8 with values in {−1, +1}. Pack later into bit-packed int1/int2 for the kernel micro-bench; keep int8 for simplicity in Python.
  - Keep per-layer scale vectors; optionally per-channel s_p to improve fidelity.

Minimal packer and centroid-upscaling sketch

  import torch, math
  class BitPlanePacker:
      def __init__(self, out_f, in_f, planes=8, device='cuda'):
          self.out_f, self.in_f, self.planes = out_f, in_f, planes
          self.B = torch.empty(planes, out_f, in_f, dtype=torch.int8, device=device)
          self.scales = torch.ones(planes, out_f, device=device, dtype=torch.float16)
      @torch.no_grad()
      def seed_from_squeezellm(self, W3, centroids):
          # W3 reconstructed 3-bit approximation, centroids implicitly define MSBs
          # Derive top-3 planes by greedy sign assignment (prototype)
          resid = W3.clone()
          for p in range(self.planes-1, self.planes-3-1, -1):
              Bp = torch.sign(resid).to(torch.int8)
              sp = (resid.abs().mean(dim=1))
              self.B[p].copy_(Bp)
              self.scales[p].copy_(sp)
              resid -= (Bp.float() * sp.unsqueeze(1))
      def state_dict(self):
          return {'B': self.B, 'scales': self.scales}

- Fine-tuning centroids/scales

  class PlaneScaleLearner(torch.nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, planes, out_f):
          super().__init__()
          self.scales = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.ones(planes, out_f, dtype=torch.float16))
      def forward(self, logits):
          return logits

- In practice we will attach per-layer packers and keep B as buffers (frozen), training only the small set of scales and controller.

HATQLinear drop-in module (shared)

  import torch
  import torch.nn as nn

  class HATQLinear(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, in_f, out_f, planes=8, device='cuda'):
          super().__init__()
          self.in_f, self.out_f, self.planes = in_f, out_f, planes
          # Frozen bit-planes as buffers
          self.register_buffer('B', torch.empty(planes, out_f, in_f, dtype=torch.int8, device=device))
          self.scales = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(planes, out_f, dtype=torch.float16, device=device), requires_grad=True)  # small trainable params
          self.min_msb = 3
          self.register_buffer('bit_counter', torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.long), persistent=False)
      def load_planes(self, B_planes, scales):
          assert B_planes.shape == self.B.shape
          self.B.copy_(B_planes)
          if scales is not None:
              with torch.no_grad(): self.scales.copy_(scales)
      def forward(self, x, token_bits=None):
          # x: [T*B, in_f] or [B, in_f]; token_bits: [T*B] ints specifying total bits for this op
          # Fallback: use fixed 4-bit if token_bits is None
          if x.dim() == 3:
              x = x.reshape(-1, x.size(-1))
          if token_bits is None:
              token_bits = torch.full((x.size(0),), 4, device=x.device, dtype=torch.int32)
          unique = torch.unique_consecutive(token_bits.sort()[0])  # small set of groups
          out = torch.empty(x.size(0), self.out_f, device=x.device, dtype=torch.float16)
          # Compute MSB floor + conditional extra planes group-by-bits
          for k in unique.tolist():
              idx = (token_bits == k).nonzero(as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
              xk = x.index_select(0, idx).to(torch.float16)
              # Planes to use: most significant k planes [planes-k, ..., planes-1]
              acc = None
              for p in range(self.planes - k, self.planes):
                  Bp = self.B[p].to(torch.float16)
                  sp = self.scales[p]
                  contrib = torch.matmul(xk, Bp.t())
                  acc = contrib * sp if acc is None else acc + contrib * sp
              out.index_copy_(0, idx, acc)
          self.bit_counter += token_bits.sum().cpu()
          return out

- Integration into HF models

  def replace_linear_with_hatq(model, planes_store):
      for name, module in list(model.named_modules()):
          for child_name, child in list(module.named_children()):
              if isinstance(child, nn.Linear):
                  hat = HATQLinear(child.in_features, child.out_features, planes=8, device=child.weight.device)
                  # Load bit-planes/scales from planes_store[name.child_name]
                  B, scales = planes_store.get(f"{name}.{child_name}")
                  hat.load_planes(B, scales)
                  setattr(module, child_name, hat)
      return model

- Effective bits accounting

  class BitStats:
      def __init__(self):
          self.total_planes = 0
          self.total_tokens = 0
      def update(self, token_bits):
          self.total_planes += int(token_bits.sum().item())
          self.total_tokens += int(token_bits.numel())
      def avg_bits(self):
          return self.total_planes / max(1, self.total_tokens)

Controller modules (shared)
- Stage A (global budget) and Stage B (per-token mask) are light. We’ll reuse last-layer hidden states to avoid KV growth.

  class GlobalBudgetRNN(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, n_layers, hist=16, hidden=128, min_bits=3, max_bits=8):
          super().__init__()
          self.gru = nn.GRU(input_size=n_layers, hidden_size=hidden, batch_first=True)
          self.out = nn.Linear(hidden, n_layers)  # per-layer budget logit
          self.min_bits, self.max_bits = min_bits, max_bits
      def forward(self, kv_stats_seq):
          # kv_stats_seq: [B, hist, n_layers], e.g., per-layer mean|var of KV over past steps
          h,_ = self.gru(kv_stats_seq)
          logits = self.out(h[:, -1])  # [B, n_layers]
          probs = torch.sigmoid(logits)
          cont = self.min_bits + (self.max_bits - self.min_bits) * probs
          hard = cont.round().clamp(self.min_bits, self.max_bits)
          return hard.detach() + (cont - cont.detach())

  class TokenMaskBlock(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, hidden_size, heads=2):
          super().__init__()
          self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_size)
          self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(hidden_size, num_heads=heads, batch_first=True)
          self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hidden_size, 4*hidden_size), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4*hidden_size, 1))
      def forward(self, last_hidden):
          # last_hidden: [B, T, H]
          x = self.ln(last_hidden)
          attn_out, _ = self.attn(x, x, x, need_weights=False)
          logits = self.mlp(attn_out).squeeze(-1)  # [B, T]
          return logits

  class BudgetHead(nn.Module):
      def __init__(self, min_bits=3, max_bits=8):
          super().__init__(); self.min_bits=min_bits; self.max_bits=max_bits
      def forward(self, global_bits_bt, token_logits_bt):
          # global_bits_bt: [B, L]; token_logits_bt: [B, T] => allocate extra bits under layer-global budgets
          probs = torch.sigmoid(token_logits_bt)  # [B, T]
          # Convert probs to 0/1 extra-bit decisions via STE rounding
          cont = probs
          if self.training:
              noise = torch.empty_like(cont).uniform_(-0.5, 0.5)
              hard01 = (cont + noise).round().clamp(0, 1)
          else:
              hard01 = cont.round().clamp(0, 1)
          hard = hard01.detach() + (cont - cont.detach())
          return hard  # [B, T] extra-bit indicator; convert to per-layer per-token outside

Latency proxy (shared)

  def latency_proxy(bits_lbt):
      # bits_lbt: [L, B*T] or [B, T, L]; mean planes per matmul
      return bits_lbt.float().mean()

Evaluation helpers (shared)

  def cuda_bench(run_fn, warmup=50, steps=200):
      start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True); end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
      for _ in range(warmup):
          run_fn()
      torch.cuda.synchronize(); torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
      start.record()
      for _ in range(steps):
          run_fn()
      end.record(); end.synchronize()
      ms = start.elapsed_time(end) / steps
      mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()
      return ms, mem


Experiment 1 — End-to-end effectiveness on accuracy, speed, memory, and average bits
Goal
- Validate that HATQ preserves static-4b accuracy while reducing average effective bits, increasing tokens/sec and lowering peak memory across tasks and sequence lengths. Also includes robustness tests and ablations.

Setup
- Models: Llama-2-7B-hf, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2.
- Quantization seed: SqueezeLLM 3-bit. Run incremental upscaling to 8-bit planes; attach HATQLinear to all linear layers (QKV/O projections, MLP up/down, gate).
- Controller: GlobalBudgetRNN + TokenMaskBlock + BudgetHead, trained jointly with plane scales on 2k sequences (length 2k) mixed-domain.
- Tasks
  - Perplexity: WikiText-2, C4 validation subsets.
  - Reasoning: MMLU (57 subjects via lm-eval harness), GSM8K 8-shot (standard prompts).
  - Commonsense: HellaSwag 10-shot.
  - Robustness: AdvBench subset (200 prompts); 32k synthetic long-context copying.
- Baselines: FP16; static 4-bit RTN; AWQ 4-bit; SqueezeLLM 3/4-bit; Any-Precision 4-bit (no dynamics); CherryQ 3-bit.

Training procedure (controller + scales)
- Data: 2k sequences sampled 25% C4, 25% Wikipedia, 25% Code (e.g., stack, github), 25% QA/dialogue.
- Objective: L = λ·NLL + (1−λ)·LatencyProxy, with λ=0.8. Straight-through discretization for token bits. Gradient clipping 1.0.
- Optimizer: AdamW lr=2e-4, wd=0.01, cosine decay to 2e-5 over 10k steps. Batch size 8; sequence length 2048.
- Implementation detail: During training, compute per-layer per-token bit targets by combining Stage A budgets and Stage B extra-bit mask; ensure MSB floor of 3. During backward, use STE to propagate into controller logits and scale parameters.

  def train_controller(model, data_loader, controller_modules, steps=10000, lambda_nll=0.8):
      gb_rnn, mask_block, budget_head = controller_modules
      optim = torch.optim.AdamW(list(model.parameters()) + list(gb_rnn.parameters()) + list(mask_block.parameters()) + list(budget_head.parameters()), lr=2e-4, weight_decay=1e-2)
      sch = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optim, T_max=steps, eta_min=2e-5)
      model.train(); gb_rnn.train(); mask_block.train(); budget_head.train()
      it = iter(data_loader)
      for step in range(steps):
          batch = next(it)  # tokenized input [B, T]
          inputs = batch["input_ids"].to(model.device)
          attn_mask = batch.get("attention_mask", None)
          # 1) Collect KV stats from past steps (mock with zeros if not maintained)
          kv_stats = torch.zeros(inputs.size(0), 16, model.config.num_hidden_layers, device=inputs.device)
          # 2) Global budgets per layer
          gbits = gb_rnn(kv_stats)  # [B, L]
          # 3) Forward to last hidden to reuse
          outputs = model.model(inputs, output_hidden_states=True, use_cache=False, return_dict=True, attention_mask=attn_mask)
          last_hidden = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [B, T, H]
          token_logits = mask_block(last_hidden)  # [B, T]
          extra_mask = budget_head(gbits, token_logits)  # [B, T] in {0,1} via STE
          # 4) Compose per-layer token bits: MSB floor 3 + extra_mask (broadcast to layers with budget constraints)
          bits_btl = torch.clamp(3 + extra_mask.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, model.config.num_hidden_layers), 3, 8)
          # 5) Apply HATQ with these bits (internal modules read a thread-local tensor)
          model._set_token_bits(bits_btl)  # you implement this setter to stash bit counts
          lm_logits = model.lm_head(outputs.last_hidden_state)
          shift_logits = lm_logits[:, :-1].contiguous()
          shift_labels = inputs[:, 1:].contiguous()
          nll = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(shift_logits.view(-1, shift_logits.size(-1)), shift_labels.view(-1), reduction='mean')
          lat = latency_proxy(bits_btl)
          loss = lambda_nll * nll + (1 - lambda_nll) * lat
          optim.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
          loss.backward(); torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
          optim.step(); sch.step()

- Practical note: To keep code minimally invasive, implement a context manager that supplies token_bits to HATQLinear modules via a thread-local variable or torch.utils._python_dispatch; or store the per-layer bit vector in each module before forward.

Inference and measurement
- Throughput/memory
  - Use decode-only measurement: fixed prompts and incremental generation; evaluate tokens/sec for total sequence lengths of 16, 128, 512 (prompt+generated). Warm up 50 steps.
  - Use CUDA graphs after warm-up to reduce launch overhead; make controller compatible with graph capture or run it on a side stream and stash bits before the GEMMs.
  - Report per-setting averages over 5 runs; compute 95% CI via bootstrap.
- Accuracy/Perplexity
  - Perplexity on WT2 and C4: teacher-forcing perplexity with model.eval(), no dropout.
  - MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag: use lm-eval-harness to avoid reimplementing protocols; pass a custom model wrapper that routes linear ops through HATQ and updates token bits per generation step.
- Robustness
  - AdvBench: run a 200-prompt subset; record refusal/behavior rates and accuracy where applicable.
  - 32k synthetic copy: prompt with a random 8–16 character key near the beginning; require exact recall at the end; score accuracy vs position and measure whether bit budgets inflate near late positions.

Experiment 2 — Systems micro-benchmarks of masked bit-plane fetch and micro-batch splitting
Goal
- Isolate kernel-level benefits: selective bit-plane loading and token grouping versus static 4-bit and naïve dynamic execution.

Setup
- Synthetic GEMMs mimicking transformer layers: shapes
  - Attention proj: (M tokens × K hidden) × (N out) with K=N=4096
  - MLP up: K=4096, N=11008; M in {32, 128, 512}
- Modes
  1) Static 4-bit: fixed 4 planes loaded for all rows.
  2) HATQ masked fetch: load MSB planes for all rows, conditionally load extra planes per row; group rows by requested bits (micro-batch split) to avoid serialization inside the kernel.
  3) Naïve dynamic: one kernel launch per precision group without further grouping (worst-case overhead).
  4) Fetch-without-optimizations: load all planes unconditionally, then mask contributions in compute.

Bit budget mixes
- Mix A: 70% 3-bit, 25% 4-bit, 5% 6-bit
- Mix B: 85% 3-bit, 10% 4-bit, 5% 7-bit
- Mix C: 10% 3-bit, 60% 4-bit, 30% 6-bit (adversarial)

Triton kernel sketch (illustrative; replace inner loops with WMMA/int8 MMA when optimizing)

  import triton
  import triton.language as tl

  @triton.jit
  def hatq_gemm_bitplanes(A_ptr, B_ptr, scales_ptr, C_ptr,
                          M, N, K, planes,
                          stride_am, stride_ak, stride_bp, stride_bn, stride_bk,
                          stride_sp, stride_sn,
                          stride_cm, stride_cn,
                          row_bits_ptr,  # [M] u32: number of planes per row
                          BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr):
      m = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
      n = tl.program_id(1) * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
      acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)
      # Determine per-row k planes
      row_bits = tl.load(row_bits_ptr + m, mask=m < M, other=0)
      # Base: process MSB planes only where needed
      for k0 in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
          a = tl.load(A_ptr + m[:, None] * stride_am + (k0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K))[None, :] * stride_ak,
                      mask=(m[:, None] < M) & (k0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K))[None, :] < K, other=0.0)
          # Iterate planes: for p in [planes - max(row_bits), planes)
          for p in range(0, planes):
              # Mask rows that don't include plane p
              need_p = (planes - row_bits) <= p
              mask_rows = need_p
              Bp = tl.load(B_ptr + p * stride_bp + n[None, :] * stride_bn + (k0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K))[:, None] * stride_bk,
                           mask=(k0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K))[:, None] < K)
              sp = tl.load(scales_ptr + p * stride_sp + n)
              contrib = tl.dot(a, Bp) * sp[None, :]
              # Zero-out rows that do not need this plane
              contrib = tl.where(mask_rows[:, None], contrib, 0.0)
              acc += contrib
      tl.store(C_ptr + m[:, None] * stride_cm + n[None, :] * stride_cn, acc, mask=(m[:, None] < M) & (n[None, :] < N))

Python driver with grouping

  def run_grouped(A, B_planes, scales, row_bits, block=128):
      # Group rows by bits for fewer distinct kernel calls
      M, K = A.shape; N = B_planes.size(1)
      C = torch.empty(M, N, device=A.device, dtype=torch.float16)
      uniq = torch.unique(row_bits)
      for k in uniq.tolist():
          idx = (row_bits == k).nonzero(as_tuple=False).squeeze(-1)
          Ak = A.index_select(0, idx).contiguous()
          Ck = torch.empty(idx.numel(), N, device=A.device, dtype=torch.float16)
          grid = (triton.cdiv(idx.numel(), block), triton.cdiv(N, block))
          hatq_gemm_bitplanes[grid](Ak, B_planes, scales, Ck,
                                    Ak.size(0), N, K, B_planes.size(0),
                                    Ak.stride(0), Ak.stride(1), B_planes.stride(0), B_planes.stride(1), B_planes.stride(2),
                                    scales.stride(0), scales.stride(1),
                                    Ck.stride(0), Ck.stride(1),
                                    torch.full((Ak.size(0),), k, dtype=torch.int32, device=A.device),
                                    BLOCK_M=block, BLOCK_N=block, BLOCK_K=block)
          C.index_copy_(0, idx, Ck)
      return C

Timing harness

  def gen_mix_bits(M, mix):
      probs = torch.tensor([mix[3], mix[4], mix.get(5,0), mix[6], mix.get(7,0)], dtype=torch.float64)
      probs = probs / probs.sum()
      choices = torch.tensor([3,4,5,6,7], dtype=torch.int32)
      return choices[torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=M, replacement=True).to(torch.long)].cuda()

  def bench_kernel(M=128, K=4096, N=4096, mix={3:0.7,4:0.25,6:0.05}, mode='hatq'):
      A = torch.randn(M, K, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
      planes = 8
      B = torch.randint(0, 2, (planes, N, K), device='cuda', dtype=torch.int8)*2-1
      scales = torch.ones(planes, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
      row_bits = gen_mix_bits(M, mix)
      def run():
          if mode=='static4':
              rb = torch.full((M,), 4, device='cuda', dtype=torch.int32)
              return run_grouped(A, B, scales, rb)
          elif mode=='hatq':
              return run_grouped(A, B, scales, row_bits)
          elif mode=='naive':
              # launch separately per row (illustrative worst-case)
              C = torch.empty(M, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
              for i in range(M):
                  C[i:i+1] = run_grouped(A[i:i+1], B, scales, row_bits[i:i+1])
              return C
          elif mode=='fetch_all_then_mask':
              rb = torch.full((M,), 8, device='cuda', dtype=torch.int32)
              C = run_grouped(A, B, scales, rb)
              # mask effect in compute (no bytes saved)
              return C
      ms, _ = cuda_bench(run)
      return ms

Protocol
- For each mix in {A, B, C} and each M in {32, 128, 512}, measure kernel ms for modes {static4, hatq, naive, fetch_all_then_mask}. Average over 200 iterations after 50 warm-up runs.
- Collect DRAM bytes read using Nsight Compute (dram__bytes_read.sum) or approximate analytically as planes_loaded × N × K × sizeof(element). Report achieved FLOPs or throughput.

Reliability practices
- Run with CUDA Graphs off to observe raw kernel performance; then repeat with graphs to assess potential improvements.
- Keep B, scales, and A fixed across modes to ensure fair comparison; only vary row_bits and control flow.
- Repeat with two different seeds for A and B to ensure findings are not data-shape idiosyncrasies.

Expected outcomes
- HATQ masked fetch reduces bytes read by 25–40% in Mix A/B, yielding ~10–20% kernel-time speedup vs static 4-bit.
- Naïve dynamic is much slower due to many small launches.
- Fetch-without-optimizations shows ~10% penalty, isolating benefit of selective loading.


Experiment 3 — Controller quality, overhead, and ablations vs heuristics
Goal
- Demonstrate that the hierarchical controller accurately identifies “hard” tokens, generalizes across domains and models, and adds negligible overhead compared to heuristics.

Setup
- Same model and training data as Experiment 1.
- Held-out diagnostic set: 500 sequences for metrics; 200 sequences for offline label creation.

Offline label creation
- For each token on a held-out set, compute ΔNLL between forced 3-bit and 3-bit+2 planes (i.e., 5-bit) for the layer with highest sensitivity; label y=1 if ΔNLL < −τ (improvement significant), with τ chosen to produce 10–20% positive rate. This approximates which tokens benefit from extra precision.

  @torch.no_grad()
  def compute_offline_labels(model, data_loader, tau=0.02):
      labels = []
      for batch in data_loader:
          x = batch["input_ids"].to(model.device)
          # NLL at 3b
          model._force_bits(3)
          logits3 = model(x).logits
          nll3 = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits3[:, :-1].reshape(-1, logits3.size(-1)), x[:, 1:].reshape(-1), reduction='none')
          nll3 = nll3.view(x.size(0), -1)
          # NLL at 5b
          model._force_bits(5)
          logits5 = model(x).logits
          nll5 = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits5[:, :-1].reshape(-1, logits5.size(-1)), x[:, 1:].reshape(-1), reduction='none')
          nll5 = nll5.view(x.size(0), -1)
          dnll = (nll5 - nll3)  # negative is improvement
          y = (dnll < -tau).int()
          labels.append(y.cpu())
      return torch.cat(labels, dim=0)

Training the controller (diagnostics-focused)
- Use the joint objective from Experiment 1; additionally monitor ROC-AUC of the per-token mask logits vs y on a dev set (labels computed offline).
- During training, capture the controller forward time:

  import time
  def measure_controller_overhead(controller, inputs):
      torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0 = time.perf_counter()
      _ = controller(*inputs)
      torch.cuda.synchronize(); t1 = time.perf_counter()
      return (t1 - t0) * 1e3  # ms

Heuristic baselines
- Norm: extra bit if ||h_t||2 above percentile p.
- Entropy: extra bit if output logit entropy > threshold.
- Gradient proxy: per-token loss increment using last-step loss or gradient norm approximations.
- Random: same positive rate as controller for calibration.

  def heuristic_policy(last_hidden, logits, mode='norm', rate=0.15):
      B, T, H = last_hidden.shape
      if mode=='norm':
          s = last_hidden.norm(dim=-1)  # [B, T]
      elif mode=='entropy':
          probs = torch.softmax(logits.detach(), dim=-1)
          s = -(probs * torch.log(probs + 1e-6)).sum(-1)
      elif mode=='random':
          s = torch.rand(B, T, device=last_hidden.device)
      # Choose top-k proportion
      k = max(1, int(rate * T))
      thresh = torch.kthvalue(s, max(1, T - k), dim=1).values.unsqueeze(1)
      mask = (s >= thresh).int()
      return mask

Diagnostics and metrics
- Token-level: ROC-AUC, Precision/Recall@k for the offline labels; compute with scikit-learn.
- End-to-end: Insert each policy into HATQ and measure accuracy-at-fixed-average-bits on WT2, MMLU-5-subset, GSM8K-500. Also measure tokens/sec at matched accuracy.
- Overhead: Report controller wall-clock per step and % of decode step.
- Generalization: Train controller on Llama-2-7B; evaluate zero-shot on Mistral-7B by plugging into the same HATQLinear structure (layer counts matched or mapped). Report degradation in ROC-AUC and end-to-end KPIs.

End-to-end harness for throughput, memory, and effective bits (integrated)

  class HATQRunner:
      def __init__(self, model, tokenizer, controller_modules):
          self.model = model.eval()
          self.tok = tokenizer
          self.gb_rnn, self.mask_block, self.budget_head = controller_modules
          self.bit_stats = BitStats()
      @torch.no_grad()
      def step_decode(self, input_ids):
          # 1) Gather KV stats (stubbed as zeros here)
          B = input_ids.size(0)
          kv_stats = torch.zeros(B, 16, self.model.config.num_hidden_layers, device=input_ids.device)
          gbits = self.gb_rnn(kv_stats)  # [B, L]
          # 2) Forward to last hidden once
          out = self.model.model(input_ids, output_hidden_states=True, use_cache=True, return_dict=True)
          last_hidden = out.hidden_states[-1]
          token_logits = self.mask_block(last_hidden)
          extra_mask = self.budget_head(gbits, token_logits)  # [B, T]
          bits_btl = torch.clamp(3 + extra_mask.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, self.model.config.num_hidden_layers), 3, 8)
          # 3) Set per-layer bits and run next-step logits
          self.model._set_token_bits(bits_btl)
          logits = self.model.lm_head(out.last_hidden_state[:, -1:])  # next token logits
          self.bit_stats.update(bits_btl.reshape(-1))
          return logits

  def run_throughput(runner, prompts, max_new_tokens=128):
      input_ids = runner.tok(prompts, return_tensors='pt', padding=True).input_ids.cuda()
      def run():
          ids = input_ids
          for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
              logits = runner.step_decode(ids)
              next_id = torch.argmax(logits[:, -1, :], dim=-1, keepdim=True)
              ids = torch.cat([ids, next_id], dim=1)
      ms, mem = cuda_bench(run)
      tps = (max_new_tokens * input_ids.size(0)) / (ms / 1000.0)
      return tps, mem, runner.bit_stats.avg_bits()


Notes and implementation tips
- Start with int8 tensor planes for clarity; once validated, switch to bit-packed storage inside Triton for better memory bandwidth.
- Use flash-attn for attention to ensure the GEMM micro-bench improvements translate to end-to-end runs (i.e., avoid attention becoming the bottleneck).
- Use CUDA Graphs in decode loops to shrink launch overhead; ensure controller ops either are captured or run outside the graph using static tensor shapes to avoid invalidation.
- When comparing tokens/sec, keep sampling strategy fixed (greedy or temperature=0) to minimize variability.
- For BitsAndBytes compatibility, expose a QuantizationConfig-like object and nn.Linear subclass compatible with HF’s load_in_8bit and device_map; register a custom weight-only quantization configuration so model.from_pretrained can instantiate HATQLinear automatically.

Risk and mitigation
- Controller over-allocates bits on OOD inputs: cap per-layer average to a safety budget; fall back to static-4b if latency budget exceeded for more than K steps.
- Kernel divergence: ensure per-group launch sizes are large enough to saturate SMs; fuse consecutive planes inside a tile to reduce memory round-trips.
- Accuracy regressions on long-context: add penalty in latency proxy that grows with bits at late positions; or allow higher budgets near attention saturation to stabilize.

Compute budget estimate (per model)
- Bit-plane scale/controller fine-tuning: ~10k steps × batch 8 × seq 2k ≈ 16M tokens; A100-80G at ~2–3k tokens/s → ~1.5–2.5 hours.
- End-to-end evaluations: lm-eval across MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag ≈ 2–3 hours/model including multiple ablations.

Together, these expanded procedures and code scaffolds should allow a reliable implementation and evaluation of HATQ across algorithmic, systems, and end-to-end dimensions while minimizing from-scratch components and ensuring reproducibility.
